reading.body:
AI risk is entering insurance as ten separate coverage questions, and three of them concern physical compute and buildings rather than data alone.

The list divides roughly in two. One half covers model behaviour: injected instructions in retrieved content, reverse engineering a model to recover training data, poisoned training data altering operational logic, staff uploading confidential material to unsanctioned tools, and synthetic media defeating biometric authentication. The other half covers infrastructure: ransomware on building control systems, compromised packages distributed through public model hubs, stolen API keys used to run unauthorised GPU workloads, zero days in widely deployed inference and orchestration frameworks, and war exclusions applied to state sponsored attacks on compute infrastructure.

Insurance language is where a risk becomes a price. Coverage written before indirect prompt injection existed decides whether an exfiltration loss is paid, and that decides how retrieval systems get deployed, how far building controls get hardened, and whether operators can carry state-linked compute risk at all. That operational technology ransomware and compute hijacking sit on the same list as model inversion says the exposure is not confined to software.

What the list does not carry is any loss figure, premium, claim count, jurisdiction, or source. It is a map of exposures the industry is naming, not evidence of what has been paid or what is actually covered. Ten categories, with nothing to say which are standard, which are exclusions, and which are still being argued.
